body:
### Motivation.

vLLM exposes `max_num_batched_tokens` (MBT) as a static scheduling configuration. For long-context workloads, however, we observe that the latency-optimal token budget depends on the current scheduling pressure.

Under low scheduling pressure, a large MBT can improve prefill execution efficiency and reduce end-to-end latency. As concurrent prefill and decode work increases, a smaller prefill budget can become preferable by limiting prefill interference with active decoding.

This means that no single static MBT is optimal across changing load regimes.

We investigated this behavior across multiple models, workloads, and NVIDIA GPUs (RTX 5090, A100, and H100), including kernel-level profiling with Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute. Based on these observations, we developed Prefill-Pressure Adaptive Scheduling (P-PAS), a lightweight policy that adapts the amount of prefill work admitted by the scheduler.

Across the main load sweep, P-PAS reduced average end-to-end latency by 8.5% relative to fixed MBT 2k and by 11.3% relative to fixed MBT 16k.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15171

Implementation, benchmarks, raw results, and profiling traces:
https://github.com/TimoSaemann/ppas-vllm

### Proposed Change.

Add an optional adaptive prefill-budget policy to the V1 scheduler.

The evaluated P-PAS policy uses scheduler state that is already available.
Let:

- `N_p` be the number of running and waiting prefill requests
- `N_d` be the number of running decode requests
- `N_th` be a prefill-pressure threshold
- `B_max` be the normal prefill token budget
- `B_cap` be the reduced prefill token budget

The policy is:

```text
if N_p >= N_th and N_d > 0:
    prefill_budget = B_cap
else:
    prefill_budget = B_max
```

For the experiments in the paper:

```text
N_th  = 2
B_max = 16384
B_cap = 2048
```

The global scheduler token budget remains unchanged. The adaptive budget only limits the aggregate amount of prefill work admitted within a scheduler iteration.

The current implementation is a small modification of the vLLM V1 scheduler and can be enabled or disabled without changing the standard scheduling behavior when disabled.

I would be happy to adapt the implementation to the current vLLM scheduler and make the policy/configuration interface consistent with the maintainers' preferred design.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

A working implementation for vLLM 0.22.1 is available in the repository linked above. If there is interest in this direction, I would be happy to adapt the implementation to the current vLLM scheduler and prepare a PR.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

comments.body:
Small update since opening this RFC:

I have ported P-PAS to vLLM 0.27.1 and evaluated it with substantially larger recent models:

- Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4
- NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4

The updated implementation, benchmark results, and vLLM 0.27.1 patch are available in a separate branch:

https://github.com/TimoSaemann/ppas-vllm/tree/vllm-0.27.1

P-PAS continues to improve latency on these models under changing serving pressure. Interestingly, the useful scheduling budgets differ considerably between the two models: the Qwen experiments use `B_max=2048, B_cap=768`, while Nemotron uses `B_max=16384, B_cap=1280`.

This RFC is adjacent to a scheduler policy I have been validating, but the
mechanism is materially different:

- P-PAS caps aggregate prefill admission when prefill/decode pressure crosses a
  threshold.
- Small-prefill batching leaves the global token budgets unchanged. While decode
  work is runnable, it defers individual text prefill chunks below a configurable
  threshold, then releases them when the combined deferred work reaches that
  threshold or a bounded scheduler-step delay expires.

The two policies should be composable: one controls the aggregate prefill budget,
while the other avoids launching sparse, inefficient prefill work. The latter is
default-off and excludes multimodal inputs.

In one serving experiment, `3072/384` at QPS 12 produced 2.462 s average E2E
versus about 2.656 s for a limited baseline comparison (roughly 7.3% lower), with
no failures, preemptions, or sustained waiting. The baseline was not a fully
matched crossover, so this is an observation rather than a capacity claim.

I have a current-`main` patch with focused scheduler/CLI tests and plan to submit
it separately. If you see a preferred integration point with P-PAS, I would be
happy to align the interfaces.

Thanks for sharing! The two approaches look conceptually compatible, although their interaction would need to be evaluated in practice. Interesting to see another approach targeting prefill scheduling.

Great to see this RFC — we independently ran into the same gap from a different direction
and have measurements that may be useful for the design discussion, plus a working
implementation of the *fixed* form of exactly the primitive this RFC needs.

**Setup.** NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, 128 GB coherent unified memory; ~121.7 GiB OS-visible
on our unit), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 (3x Gated DeltaNet + 1x Gated Attention, 256-expert MoE),
single V1 engine, sustained contention from 8 concurrent 16K-token prefill loops against a
decode workload (128-in/512-out). Protocol pre-registered with the analysis frozen before
results; repeat-cell noise 4.96%.

**A static sweep of the primitive.** We implemented an aggregate per-step prefill token
budget (`max_prefill_tokens_per_step`, default off; the global token budget is unchanged —
i.e. the same quantity your policy adapts as B_cap/B_max) and swept it:

| aggregate prefill budget | decode TPOT tax (C=4)* | 16K prefills/min | TTFT p50 (C=16) |
|---|---|---|---|
| off | 11.7x (438 ms) | 14.8 | 27.1 s |
| 2048 | 11.7x (441 ms) | 15.0 | 27.2 s |
| 1024 | 7.5x (282 ms) | 11.4 | 34.4 s |
| 512 | 6.2x (232 ms) | 7.0 | 54.9 s |
| 256 | 4.8x (179 ms) | 4.8 | 80.0 s |

*decode TPOT under contention at C=4, normalized by a batch-matched C=4 decode-alone
baseline (37.6 ms median TPOT, measured on the same engine config; the large baseline gap vs decode-alone at C=16 — 104.6 ms — is itself an MoE batch effect on this hardware).

Two observations that seem directly relevant to the adaptive policy:

1. **The tradeoff is large and monotonic on this hardware class** — the budget sweeps
   decode tax 11.7x -> 4.8x (438 -> 179 ms/token) against a 15 -> 5/min prefill-throughput cost and
   27 -> 80 s TTFT. Unified-memory devices (GB10 etc.) may be an extreme point of the
   pressure regime your policy targets, so they could be a useful stress test for B_cap
   selection.
2. **Which metric hurts depends on decode occupancy, not only prefill pressure.** With
   free decode slots (C=4) the cost of an uncapped budget shows up in decode TPOT
   (continuous interleave); with full slots (C=16) per-token metrics stay clean and the
   entire cost moves into TTFT/admission (phase alternation: prompt-only steps against
   decode-only bursts). A pressure signal that looks at N_d relative to slot capacity —
   not just N_d > 0 — might let P-PAS pick which side to protect.

**Offer.** If it helps this RFC land, we're glad to contribute the static primitive as a
PR (`[Core] Add a fixed aggregate prefill budget per scheduler iteration`, default-off,
config-plumbed, with unit tests including the preemption-refund interaction) so P-PAS can
build on it as the manual mode / the mechanism its policy drives. Entirely happy to align
naming and interface with whatever design you and the maintainers prefer — treating this
RFC as the design home for the policy question.

Raw data, scripts, and engine logs available on request.

---
AI-assisted disclosure: implementation and measurement harness developed with Claude Code
under human direction; protocols pre-registered and all numbers re-derived from raw bench
JSONs by hand before posting.

Thanks for sharing these measurements and the offer! It is great to see on the DGX Spark/GB10 that changing the aggregate prefill budget exposes the same fundamental TPOT/TTFT trade-off that underlies P-PAS, despite the very different hardware and workload setup.

The main difference is the optimization objective. P-PAS uses this trade-off to minimize request-level E2E latency under changing serving pressure, rather than primarily protecting decode TPOT. In our experiments, the latency-optimal token budget changes with the workload, which is what motivates adapting the budget dynamically.

Regarding the proposed static primitive and how the mechanism and policy should be structured upstream, I think it would be best to get maintainer feedback on the preferred design before committing to a particular interface or implementation.

Follow-up after a matched 2x2 test on RTX PRO 5000 (same workload/runtime, 120s warmup + 600s measurement):

- baseline: 3,630 QPH/GPU
- Small Prefill: 3,699 (+1.90%)
- P-PAS: 3,606 (-0.66%)
- combined: 3,438 (-5.29% vs. baseline, -7.06% vs. Small Prefill)

There were no failures or preemptions. I should therefore correct my earlier “should be composable” wording: the mechanisms are distinct, but their gains are not necessarily additive; in this setup they double-throttled prefill admission. #54145 now documents this interaction.

Update on the evaluation:

I extended P-PAS to heterogeneous workloads with P-PAS+, which adds an additional pressure condition for cases where a single large running prefill overlaps with multiple decode requests.

I evaluated it on NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 with 20 request shapes spanning 16k–131k prompt tokens and 16–256 output tokens, across different request rates and burst durations.

The evaluation required ~18 GPU hours and covered 1,045 matched requests. P-PAS+ reduced workload-level mean E2E latency by 3.1% compared with the best tested static token budget (MBT 1280) and achieved lower E2E latency for 88.5% of individual requests.

Updated implementation, evaluation scripts, raw results, and vLLM 0.27.1 patch:
https://github.com/TimoSaemann/ppas-vllm/tree/ppas-plus

Final update: the revised P-PAS paper is now available on arXiv and includes the P-PAS+ heterogeneous evaluation.

P-PAS+ was evaluated on:
- Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4: 3.0% lower mean E2E latency vs. the best tested static budget; 91.2% of matched requests faster
- Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4: 3.1% lower mean E2E latency; 88.5% of matched requests faster

The evaluation covers prompt lengths from 8k to 128k tokens and output lengths from 16 to 256 tokens under changing serving pressure.

Revised paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15171
Implementation, benchmarks, and raw results: https://github.com/TimoSaemann/ppas-vllm

title: [RFC]: Adaptive prefill token budget based on scheduling pressure
